metadata.title: Conditioning evidence source and model manifest
metadata.citation_policy: Peer-reviewed direct evidence first; peer-reviewed adjacent evidence second; official manufacturer/coaching guidance third; product-design recommendations explicitly labelled.
metadata.copyright_note: This manifest preserves article metadata, direct URLs/DOIs, evidence notes, and limitations. It does not redistribute full copyrighted article text or PDFs.

evidence_legend.A_direct: The study used the relevant modality or a clearly identified combined upper-and-lower-body ergometer.
evidence_legend.B_adjacent: The study informs a mechanism or method but used a different modality, body configuration, or device class.
evidence_legend.C_guidance: Official manufacturer, governing-body, or coaching guidance; useful for operation or templates, not validation by itself.
evidence_legend.D_design: Product recommendation made because direct evidence is absent; must be piloted and labelled in implementation.

research_models.name: Threshold model
research_models.description: Use VT1/LT1 and VT2/LT2 as individual physiological anchors when measured. Fixed HRmax percentages are proxies, not interchangeable threshold boundaries.
valid_for: all modalities when thresholds are measured or carefully individualised
not_valid_for: automatic FTP transfer to air bike

research_models.name: HRmax and HRR proxy model
research_models.description: Use %HRmax or %HRR as broad internal-load guides, mainly for continuous work. The exact protocol, sensor, recovery mode, and modality matter.

research_models.name: Perceived-exertion model
research_models.description: RPE is an internal-load control that can be used when HR is unavailable or delayed. The scale must be explicit: Borg 6–20 and CR10 are different instruments.
not_valid_for: pretending a CR10 band is a universal threshold without calibration

research_models.name: Coggan cycling power model
research_models.description: FTP-relative power levels are a conventional cycling control system. They require cycling-specific FTP context and must not be assigned to combined arm-and-leg air bike.
valid_for: conventional cycling with a known protocol-specific FTP or threshold

research_models.name: Session-RPE load
research_models.description: Session duration in minutes multiplied by post-session RPE. Use for internal-load trend and cross-modality description, not proof of adaptation.
valid_for: all modalities when the RPE scale is explicit
not_valid_for: equating console calories or raw watts across devices
inferring injury risk from one number

research_models.name: External-load model
research_models.description: Track what was completed: time, distance, pace, watts, RPM, calories, work, strokes, or repetitions. Preserve the raw unit and device/protocol metadata.

research_models.name: Autoregulated three-outcome state machine
research_models.description: Advance only after target work, RPE, technique, symptoms, and recent comparable exposure support it; otherwise repeat or reduce. Distinguish failed execution from absence and sensor failure.
research_models.status: Product design grounded in training-load and monitoring literature; no publication validates the exact app transition counts.

research_models.name: Device-specific benchmark model
research_models.description: A benchmark is portable only when device, protocol, familiarisation, warm-up, recovery, and output metric are matched or a calibration study supports conversion.
not_valid_for: brand-to-brand calorie, watt, RPM, speed, or distance comparisons by default

research_models.name: HRR trend model
research_models.description: HRR can be retained as a standardised personal trend. Do not use the clinical 12 bpm cut-off as an athletic progression gate.

cross_reference_decisions.decision: Create air_bike as a separate modality with combined_arm_leg_fan and lower_body_air_braked subtypes.
Physiological stress can be broadly similar while console distance/calories differ; require device-specific baselines and never assume Airdyne, Assault, Echo, or Beast output portability.

Call the combined test an AssaultBike/air-bike maximal test, not a Wingate equivalent. The 60-second AssaultBike test and 30-second lower-body Wingate differ in duration, muscle configuration, lactate kinetics, and standardisation.
For Air Bike PRO-like intermittent classes, RPE was more similar to external-load control than HR; use RPE and completed work, with HR as supporting data.
Interpret peak air-bike ramp output as a whole-body performance result influenced by strength and fat-free mass, not as a pure VO2 or cycling-FTP proxy.
Block automatic Coggan FTP zones for air bike. Use RPE, duration, work completion, device-specific output, and optional lab/device threshold anchors.
Describe combined air bike as capable of high cardiovascular/metabolic stress, with the magnitude dependent on device, protocol, body configuration, and training status.
Record local limiter and separate mechanical completion from cardiovascular response. HR is secondary for short bouts.
cross_reference_decisions.inference: The specific local-fatigue-before-HR mechanism is plausible and operationally important, but is not yet quantified robustly on modern AssaultBike/Echo/Airdyne devices.

cross_reference_decisions.decision: Report acute responses and short interventions as promising; do not claim long-term superiority over other modalities.
Use lower-impact/non-weight-bearing wording, not universally safer wording. Injury incidence evidence is absent.
5-minute, 10-minute max-calorie, 2-mile, and informal Wingate-style tests are optional same-device tests, not universal validated standards.
10/5 and 20/10 have direct recreationally-active intervention evidence; Echo 15/45 and 40/20 variants have small active-adult evidence; direct beginner evidence for 30/30 and 60/60 is absent.
No evidence supports a fixed air-bike progression rate relative to running, rowing, SkiErg, or conventional cycling. Use local-fatigue-aware autoregulation.
Keep HRR as a trend; never use the clinical 12 bpm cut-off as a self-directed progression gate.
Do not encode 10% as a universal injury-prevention rule.
A default of 2–3 comparable successful exposures may be used as a product heuristic, but no universal published session count exists.

source_registry.citation: Schlegel, Health benefits of using air biking: a systematic review
source_registry.population_or_scope: 26 selected air-bike studies from 65 full-text candidates; testing and intervention evidence
key_numbers: air-bike design differences in flywheel resistance, mechanical inertia, and handle design
supports: high HR/VO2/ventilation/RER/lactate responses
device-design non-comparability
limited long-term intervention evidence
source_registry.limitations: Review includes heterogeneous devices and protocols; not a universal prescription study.

source_registry.citation: Nagle, Richie & Giese, VO2max responses in separate and combined arm and leg air-braked ergometer exercise
source_registry.population_or_scope: 10 healthy males; separate and combined arm/leg air-braked exercise
key_numbers: maximum power and VO2 response reported for arm/leg ratios; review summary identifies approximately 10% arms/90% legs as best in that protocol
supports: whole-body air-braked physiological demand
source_registry.limitations: Old device and small male sample; not AssaultBike/Echo/Airdyne validation.

source_registry.citation: Hoffman et al., Does the amount of exercising muscle alter the aerobic demand of dynamic exercise?
source_registry.population_or_scope: 9 healthy adults; leg cycling versus combined arm-and-leg Airdyne
key_numbers: combined VO2 averaged about 0.04 L/min higher than leg cycling at matched external power in the reported comparison
supports: large muscle mass can alter aerobic demand
source_registry.limitations: Tiny sample and older Airdyne; not a modern cross-brand calibration study.

source_registry.citation: Hill et al., The validity and reproducibility of perceptually regulated exercise responses during combined arm + leg cycling
source_registry.population_or_scope: 12 young men; two modified Monark ergometers; RPE 9, 13, 17
key_numbers: no significant trial differences for HR, VO2, or ventilation
RPE was a reliable intensity-production frame
supports: RPE-based control in combined arm/leg work
source_registry.limitations: Not a commercial Assault/Echo console; male sample; formal familiarisation was not the same as modern fan-bike onboarding.

source_registry.citation: Canário-Lemos et al., Validity and reliability of maximum oxygen uptake on an Air Bike arm- and leg-ergometer
source_registry.population_or_scope: 18 physically active young men; Air Bike Revolution and Wattbike leg cycle
key_numbers: Air Bike VO2max 53.06±8.72 vs leg cycle 47.38±9.15 mL/kg/min
Air Bike HRmax 181.93±10.20 vs cycle 176.07±5.28 bpm
Air Bike protocol 30 RPM then +5 RPM/min
supports: device-specific VO2 reliability
combined and leg-cycle outputs are not equivalent
source_registry.limitations: One Air Bike Revolution model; active young men; comparison is not cross-brand calibration.

source_registry.citation: Pearson, Garcia & Jenkins, Comparison of a ramp cycle ergometer and a staged Assault Fitness AssaultBike protocol for the assessment of VO2max
source_registry.population_or_scope: 12 healthy males; traditional cycle ramp versus staged AssaultBike
key_numbers: AssaultBike produced higher immediate post-exercise lactate, VO2max, and HRmax than traditional cycle; p=.006, .014, .007, and .001 reported for relevant outcomes
supports: combined device can produce different acute responses than leg cycle
source_registry.limitations: No test-retest reliability; small all-male sample; comparison does not prove superiority.

source_registry.citation: Lipscomb et al., Agreement of Air Bike and Treadmill Protocols To Assess Maximal Oxygen Uptake
source_registry.population_or_scope: 15 healthy adults; Rogue Echo Bike and treadmill; 7 had regular air-bike familiarity
key_numbers: treadmill minus air-bike bias about 3.31 mL/kg/min overall
bias about 1.27 in regular users versus 5.09 in non-regular users
supports: device-specific VO2 agreement can be good
familiarisation matters
no universal prediction equation
source_registry.limitations: Exploratory sample; agreement is not test-retest reliability; Echo Bike only.

source_registry.citation: Moghaddam et al., Sprint Interval Training on Stationary Air Bike Elicits Cardiorespiratory Adaptations While Being Time-Efficient
source_registry.population_or_scope: 32 recreationally active adults; 3 sessions/week for 4 weeks
key_numbers: 10/5 set recovery 2.5 min; 20/10 set recovery 5 min
VO2max improvements roughly 12–15% across groups as reported
supports: short air-bike SIT can improve cardiorespiratory outcomes in recreationally active adults
source_registry.limitations: Not absolute beginners; four weeks; study device/protocol and console calories do not create universal training zones.

source_registry.citation: Schlegel, Křehký & Hiblbauer, Physical fitness improvement after 8 weeks of high-intensity interval training with air bike
source_registry.population_or_scope: 20/22 healthy active young adults; Echo Bike; 2 sessions/week for 8 weeks
key_numbers: ramp starting values 40 RPM/85 W men and 35 RPM/65 W women were author protocol choices
supports: short air-bike interval training can improve fitness in active young adults
source_registry.limitations: Small active sample; protocol-specific; not beginner validation or proof of long-term superiority.

source_registry.citation: Hwang et al., Novel all-extremity high-intensity interval training improves aerobic fitness, cardiac function and insulin resistance in healthy older adults
source_registry.population_or_scope: 51 sedentary healthy older adults; supervised non-weight-bearing all-extremity ergometer
supports: supervised longer all-extremity intervals can be feasible in selected older adults
source_registry.limitations: Not necessarily modern Assault/Echo/Airdyne; supervised older sample; not self-directed beginner evidence.

source_registry.citation: Hwang et al., Effect of all-extremity high-intensity interval training vs. moderate-intensity continuous training in adults with type 2 diabetes
source_registry.population_or_scope: 58 sedentary adults with type 2 diabetes, approximately 46–78 years; supervised all-extremity ergometer
key_numbers: VO2peak improved about 10% in HIIT and 8% in MICT
supports: supervised all-extremity training can be feasible in a selected clinical population
source_registry.limitations: Not a commercial fan-bike validation; clinical and supervised population; cannot imply universal safety.

source_registry.citation: Astorino & Emma, Differences in Physiological and Perceptual Responses to High Intensity Interval Exercise Between Arm and Leg Cycling
source_registry.population_or_scope: 23 active adults without arm-exercise experience; separate arm and leg cycling
key_numbers: 10 × 1 min at 75% PPO with 1 min active recovery
mean HR around 149±14 leg versus 131±17 arm
HR and VO2 rose across repeated bouts
supports: body configuration changes HR/VO2 response
HR is not an immediate short-bout completion signal
source_registry.limitations: Not combined air bike; use as mechanism/transfer caution only.

source_registry.citation: Maxwell et al., Dynamic calibration of mechanically, air- and electromagnetically braked cycle ergometers
source_registry.population_or_scope: 35 friction, 5 research-grade air-braked, and 5 electromagnetic cycle ergometers
key_numbers: Repco air-braked accuracy approximately 98.0–100.2% over 272.7–1137.8 W
air-braked power depends strongly on cadence and environmental correction
supports: accurate output requires calibration
raw watts are device-specific
source_registry.limitations: Research-grade lower-body ergometers from 1998; no modern combined fan-bike calibration.

source_registry.citation: Driss, The Measurement of Maximal (Anaerobic) Power Output on a Cycle Ergometer: The Wingate Test
source_registry.population_or_scope: Classic Wingate methodology and its reliability/validity literature
key_numbers: commonly 7.5% body mass braking force on Monark
supports: what a standard Wingate actually is
source_registry.limitations: Does not validate a combined fan-bike Wingate.

source_registry.citation: Livingston, Reliability Of Staged Maximal Aerobic Capacity Protocol Using A Combined Upper- And Lower-Body Air-Braked Ergometer
source_registry.population_or_scope: 15 recreationally active adults; Rogue Echo Bike V3.0; one familiarisation plus two trials separated by at least 72 h
key_numbers: relative VO2peak ICC .909; absolute ICC .938; peak power ICC .966
relative VO2peak CV 7.86%; absolute CV 8.57%; peak power CV 7.87%
RER poorly reliable; verification criterion achieved in 63.3% of all sessions
supports: device-specific Echo Bike staged VO2peak protocol can be reliable in recreationally active adults
source_registry.limitations: Master's thesis, not peer-reviewed journal evidence; one model; small sample.

source_registry.citation: AssaultBike Classic owner’s manual
source_registry.population_or_scope: AssaultBike operation, display metrics, target-HR and interval programmes
supports: device operation and available metrics
source_registry.limitations: Not a validation or injury study; age-predicted HRmax and product design.

source_registry.citation: Rogue Echo Bike user guide
source_registry.population_or_scope: Echo Bike display metrics and target-HR operation
supports: device operation and available metrics
source_registry.limitations: Manual copy; not a validation or injury study.

source_registry.citation: Foster et al., session-RPE method
supports: simple internal-load model
source_registry.limitations: Does not determine adaptation or modality equivalence.

source_registry.citation: Foster, Rodríguez-Marroyo & de Koning, monitoring internal and external training load
supports: use both internal and external load
source_registry.limitations: Does not validate the app’s exact state transitions.

source_registry.citation: Impellizzeri et al., ACWR critique
supports: avoid using ACWR as a simple individual injury gate
source_registry.limitations: Methodological critique rather than an air-bike study.

source_registry.citation: Saw et al., monitoring training response and subjective wellness
supports: use symptoms and subjective context as advisory inputs
source_registry.limitations: Does not establish a universal readiness cutoff.

source_registry.citation: Cole et al., heart-rate recovery and mortality
source_registry.population_or_scope: Clinical cohort and a defined exercise/recovery protocol
key_numbers: abnormal HRR was a fall of 12 bpm or less in the first minute under the study protocol
supports: clinical prognostic meaning under a specific protocol
source_registry.limitations: Not a healthy-athlete or self-directed training gate.

source_registry.citation: Costa et al., short-term HRR test-retest reliability
source_registry.population_or_scope: 12 healthy moderately active men after maximal treadmill tests
key_numbers: reported prior SEM ranges 1.6–11.4 bpm submaximal and 3.0–10.2 bpm maximal
supports: HRR can be repeatable under a standardised protocol but has meaningful noise
source_registry.limitations: Small lab sample, treadmill, not phone/strap real-world air-bike monitoring.

source_registry.citation: Daanen et al., HRR in athletes and trained populations
supports: HRR is affected by intensity, duration, posture, temperature, age, and protocol
source_registry.limitations: No self-directed consumer-app cut-off.

source_registry.citation: Chen, Fan & Moe, meta-analysis of Borg RPE validity
source_registry.population_or_scope: RPE relationships with HR, lactate, and oxygen uptake
supports: RPE has criterion-related validity but heterogeneous mappings
source_registry.limitations: Not air-bike-specific; does not create universal CR10 bands.

source_registry.citation: Scherr et al., RPE and physiological intensity in 2,560 adults
key_numbers: RPE relationships with HR and physiological intensity were meaningful but overlapped
supports: RPE is useful but imprecise at individual thresholds
source_registry.limitations: Not air-bike-specific.

source_registry.citation: Grummt et al., RPE anchors in cardiopulmonary exercise testing
key_numbers: median Borg RPE about 13 at 2 mmol/L, 15 at 3 mmol/L, 16 at 4 mmol/L, and 15 at LT2 in the reported dataset
supports: RPE-to-threshold mappings are population-dependent
source_registry.limitations: Not air-bike-specific and not a universal prescription table.

source_registry.citation: Arney et al., RPE, CR10, and HR response during interval exercise
source_registry.population_or_scope: Interval exercise intensity labels and RPE/HR relationships
key_numbers: CR10 about 3.1/6.5/8.9 in the reported protocol
supports: RPE scales can be mapped operationally but are protocol/population dependent
source_registry.limitations: Not air-bike-specific; values should not be presented as universal air-bike bands.

source_registry.citation: ACSM aerobic exercise intensity infographic
supports: broad public exercise-intensity education
source_registry.limitations: Not air-bike-specific thresholds.

source_registry.citation: Concept2 heart-rate training guidance
supports: practical HR display convention
source_registry.limitations: Not an air-bike-specific validation; zone terminology varies.

source_registry.citation: Coggan cycling power levels
supports: cycling-specific power-zone control
source_registry.limitations: Not validated for combined arm-and-leg air bike; FTP estimate depends on protocol.

source_registry.citation: Buist et al., graded versus standard novice running programme
supports: 10% rule did not reduce injury in this trial
source_registry.limitations: Running only; does not give an air-bike progression rate.

source_registry.citation: Nielsen et al., novice running load progression and injury
source_registry.population_or_scope: 874 healthy novice runners; 202 injuries over one year
key_numbers: >30% group versus <10% group HR 1.59, 95% CI .96–2.66, p=.07
supports: large spikes may be concerning but do not establish a safe cutoff
source_registry.limitations: Running only; observational.

source_registry.citation: Damsted et al., systematic review of changes in running load and injury
supports: limited support for universal sudden-load rules
source_registry.limitations: Running only.

source_registry.citation: Ramskov et al., volume-focused versus intensity-focused running progression
supports: no clear injury-risk winner between volume-first and intensity-first progression in the study
source_registry.limitations: Running only.

source_registry.citation: NHS Couch to 5K
supports: a concrete beginner template
source_registry.limitations: Programme guidance, not proof of universal readiness thresholds.

source_registry.citation: Daniels, Daniels’ Running Formula, 3rd edition
supports: running intensity categories and progression structure
source_registry.limitations: Coaching framework; exact paces require individualisation.

source_registry.citation: Fleckenstein et al., interval structure and time above VO2max
source_registry.population_or_scope: Highly trained runners; 4×3 min versus 24×30 s interval structures
key_numbers: 4×3 min at 95% vVO2max with 3 min recovery versus 24×30 s at 100% vVO2max with 30 s recovery
supports: HR-zone time is a poor sole proxy for short-interval stimulus
source_registry.limitations: Highly trained runners; not air-bike-specific.

source_registry.citation: British Rowing Go Row beginner training plan
key_numbers: progression from 1 min low/1 min rest ×5 through medium/high pieces and a 2k
supports: concrete rowing beginner template
source_registry.limitations: Template, not a universal injury/readiness threshold.

source_registry.citation: Concept2 stroke-rate guidance
supports: rate context, not rate-as-intensity
source_registry.limitations: Not a universal pace table or air-bike transfer.

source_registry.citation: Concept2 training plans and test options
key_numbers: published 2k plans use 3 sessions/week with optional fourth in a 12-week plan; multiple distance/time tests exist
supports: benchmark protocol metadata and practical schedules
source_registry.limitations: Not an air-bike progression study.

source_registry.citation: Concept2 beginner SkiErg programme
key_numbers: 1 min hard/1 min easy, 30/30, 250 m, 1000 m, 1500 m, 2000 m progressions
supports: concrete SkiErg beginner template
source_registry.limitations: Not direct evidence for a slower progression rate than other modalities.

source_registry.citation: Concept2 SkiErg technique
supports: full-body/trunk/lat/hip-hinge movement description
source_registry.limitations: Not an injury-incidence study.

source_registry.citation: British Cycling novice 8-week sofa-to-50km plan
key_numbers: 3 rides/week; approximately 1.5 to 6.5 hours weekly across the plan
supports: concrete cycling beginner template
source_registry.limitations: Coaching plan, not a validated universal 10% rule.

source_registry.citation: TrainingPeaks FTP calculation guidance
supports: cycling software convention
source_registry.limitations: Not a universal threshold or air-bike method.

source_registry.citation: TrainerRoad ramp-test guidance
key_numbers: approximately 75% of highest one-minute power convention
supports: cycling software convention
source_registry.limitations: Not an air-bike method.

source_registry.citation: Inglis et al., FTP estimate and maximal lactate steady state
key_numbers: MLSS averaged 93.1±5.1% of FTP estimated by 20-minute × .95 in the reported sample
supports: FTP95 is an estimate with individual error
source_registry.limitations: Conventional cycling; not air bike.

source_registry.citation: Karsten et al., FTP and MLSS agreement
supports: FTP can correlate with threshold while individual limits of agreement remain meaningful
source_registry.limitations: Conventional cycling; not air bike.

source_registry.citation: Frandsen et al., single-session running-load spike and injury
key_numbers: study examined whether a single session exceeding the longest run in the preceding 30 days by at least 10% was associated with injury
supports: promising but not a universal safe cutoff
source_registry.limitations: Running only; observational; does not transfer to air bike.

source_registry.citation: Zhu et al., experience and double-poling oxygen cost
key_numbers: experienced skiers showed approximately 21% lower oxygen cost during submaximal double-poling in the reported comparison
supports: technique/economy matters in upper-body Nordic work
source_registry.limitations: Not a beginner progression or injury-tolerance study.

source_registry.citation: Sunde et al., upper-body/nordic training evidence
supports: upper-body strength and technique are relevant to Nordic work
source_registry.limitations: Does not establish beginner SkiErg loading relative to running or rowing.

source_registry.citation: Fit at Midlife, example AssaultBike workout/test catalogue
source_registry.population_or_scope: Popular gym benchmarks including 5-minute, 10-minute max calories, and 2-mile examples
key_numbers: catalogue lists the formats but does not validate them
supports: existence/popularity of tests
source_registry.limitations: No peer-reviewed validity/reliability; do not use as universal standards.

source_registry.citation: Vanderburgh, The 10-min Cycle Ergometer Test
supports: a 10-minute lower-body cycle test is not automatically a combined fan-bike test
source_registry.limitations: Not modern combined AssaultBike/Echo/Airdyne validation.

source_registry.citation: Driller, Argus & Shing, reliability of a 30-second Wattbike sprint
supports: a standardised lower-body sprint can be reliable
source_registry.limitations: Not a combined arm-and-leg fan-bike validation.

source_registry.citation: Schlegel, Křehký & Taufmann, Comparison of air bikes and their effect on selected physiological parameters
source_registry.population_or_scope: 10 physically active men; Assault, Echo, and Beast; 6-minute RPE-3, 10-minute, and 30-second protocols
key_numbers: 10-minute distance: Beast 7258.1±403.7 m, Echo 6723.8±383.6 m, Assault 6823.5±401.9 m
supports: device-specific output baselines
similar broad physiological stress with different exported distance/calorie values
source_registry.limitations: Airdyne was not included; no test-retest reliability; small active male sample; authors call for confirmation.

source_registry.citation: Schlegel & Křehký, Anaerobic fitness testing in CrossFit
source_registry.population_or_scope: 12 competitive male CrossFit athletes; 60-second AssaultBike test and 30-second lower-body Wingate one week apart
supports: a combined 60-second test is physiologically different from Wingate
air-bike test is not standardised
source_registry.limitations: Competitive male CrossFit sample; no test-retest reliability; different duration and body configuration; original study requires confirmation.

source_registry.citation: Canário-Lemos et al., Control of the intensity of effort: heart rate or rate of perceived effort
source_registry.population_or_scope: 10 physically active young men; randomized 30-minute Air Bike PRO sessions
key_numbers: External-load control anchored to ventilatory thresholds and 90% peak VO2
RPE-controlled VO2 was more similar to external-load control than HR-controlled VO2
supports: RPE can be a practical controller
HR control can underdose intended oxygen demand in class-like intermittent work
source_registry.limitations: One Air Bike Revolution format; active young men; no universal CR10-to-threshold mapping; acute study.

source_registry.citation: Schlegel, Křehký, Hiblbauer & Faltys, Air biking as a new way for stress testing
source_registry.population_or_scope: 20 physically active adults; three-minute-stage air-bike ramp to failure
key_numbers: performance correlations: fat-free mass .86, back squat .83, bench press .84, 2-km row .85, VO2peak .68
supports: air-bike ramp stress is feasible
strength and fat-free mass contribute materially to performance
source_registry.limitations: No test-retest reliability; small active sample; not a universal aerobic-capacity or progression test.

source_registry.citation: Ponce-García et al., The Anaerobic Power Assessment in CrossFit Athletes
source_registry.population_or_scope: CrossFit athletes; AssaultBike test and conventional Wingate comparison context
supports: a combined AssaultBike anaerobic test is a distinct task from lower-body Wingate
source_registry.limitations: Does not establish a universal combined-air-bike benchmark or reliability package.

evidence_gaps: No universal combined-air-bike zones by %HRmax, %HRR, CR10, VT/LT, RPM, watts, calories/min, or distance.
No validated cross-brand mapping for AssaultBike, Echo Bike, Airdyne, Air Bike Revolution, and comparable machines.
No modern combined-air-bike validity/reliability package for the popular 30-second, 1-minute, repeated-sprint, 5-minute, 10-minute, 2-mile, or Wingate-style tests.
No modern combined-air-bike critical-power or maximal-aerobic-power standard.
No direct epidemiologic incidence study located for air-bike shoulder, elbow, rib, lumbar, hip, or overuse injuries.
No evidence-based fixed air-bike progression rate relative to running, rowing, SkiErg, or conventional cycling.
No direct beginner evidence located for all requested 10/5, 20/10, 30/30, 60/60, and longer air-bike formats.
No validated universal session count before phase advancement.
No evidence that a single HRR threshold from a consumer sensor is suitable as a progression gate.
